paragraphs: The paper examines how a visual system can recognize relationships between objects built from shared parts arranged differently. It proposes a unified framework for representing visual structure in primate vision, then derives a model that can interpret and associate objects connected by these rearrangements.

The model represents parts as image fragments at an intermediate scale. Its receptive fields combine information about what appears with information about where it appears, while attention changes the strength of responses. Together, these mechanisms address the compositional problem: representing both the pieces of an object and their arrangement.

The stated result is effective systematicity: the model can connect related arrangements of common parts without requiring earlier exposure to each part individually. It also avoids requiring an abstract symbolic mechanism to bind parts together. This matters because it offers a way to explain structured visual representation using receptive fields and attentional modulation, with the demonstrated capability centered on relationships among rearranged image fragments.
neurips-2000-a-productive-systematic-fra.tldr: A visual model combines part identity, location, and attention to associate objects formed by rearranging shared image fragments.

paragraphs: A neuron in visual area V4 can receive information about several features within its receptive field. Recordings suggest that simultaneously presented stimuli compete to determine its firing rate, and that attention shifts this competition toward an attended object. The paper asks whether the organization of inputs within a single neuron could explain both effects.

The proposed architecture separates incoming synapses across different regions of an excitable dendritic tree. Under a Hebbian organizing rule, excitatory inputs with similar receptive fields cluster together while avoiding randomly positioned inhibitory inputs with similar receptive fields. The same organizing principle applies to inputs carrying attentional modulation.

The authors examine this architecture using both detailed biophysical compartment models and simpler models of single-neuron computation. Their results show that the arrangement could account for V4 response properties and attentional effects. This supports nonlinear dendritic activity as a possible contributor to visual processing beyond primary visual cortex; it does not establish that this architecture is the biological cause.
neurips-2000-dendritic-compartmentalizat.tldr: Models suggest that spatially organized dendritic inputs could explain stimulus competition and attentional biasing in V4 neurons.

paragraphs: The paper connects a pattern in human contrast perception with the behavior of a simple spiking neuron. Observers judged differences in the contrast of peripheral Gabor patches while other, collinear Gabor patches appeared nearby. These flankers produced an interaction that changed with the target's contrast.

To explain the behavioral measurements, the authors assume that flankers divide down the target unit's response at low target contrasts but subtract from it at higher contrasts. These descriptions capture different ways inhibition can alter a response: changing its scale or reducing it by an offset.

A similar transition appears in an integrate-and-fire model when inhibition varies over time, alternating between relatively high and low states. The correspondence matters because one temporal inhibition mechanism can produce both response patterns. The authors suggest that this neuronal behavior may cause the perceptual effect, while keeping that causal link tentative. The model also produces predictions that could be tested through recordings from individual neurons.
neurips-2000-divisive-and-subtractive-ma.tldr: Time-varying inhibition in a spiking neuron reproduces a contrast-dependent switch resembling measured visual masking effects.

paragraphs: The paper introduces a way to represent covariance in Gaussian mixture models and hidden Markov models. Covariance describes how modeled quantities vary together. The starting point is semi-tied covariance modeling, an efficient approach used in speech recognition that shares some structure across model components while retaining differences between them.

In the standard approach, a widely shared transform removes correlations, and each component has its own diagonal covariance matrix. The proposed method factors the shared transform into constituent pieces. This increases the number of available transforms without increasing the number of free parameters, allowing more transform choices within the same parameter budget.

The authors provide maximum-likelihood procedures for estimating component parameters, transform parameters, and the assignment of components to transforms. They evaluate the resulting model on a large-vocabulary speech recognition task and report a reduction in word error rate. The finding connects the more flexible covariance representation to improved recognition in that evaluation, while the factoring supplies the central mechanism for controlling parameter count.
neurips-2000-factored-semi-tied-covarian.tldr: Factoring shared covariance transforms expands modeling choices without adding free parameters and reduces speech recognition word error in the reported evaluation.

paragraphs: The paper proposes suppressing speech noise by estimating how much useful signal is present relative to noise in individual frequency channels. This local signal-to-noise ratio determines how strongly each channel is attenuated, making the estimate a central part of the suppression process.

To obtain those estimates, the input is converted into Amplitude Modulation Spectrograms. These describe both spectral content and temporal variation within an analysis frame. The representation is motivated by how higher stages of the mammalian auditory system represent modulation frequencies. A neural network analyzes patterns in these spectrograms from noisy speech and estimates the local signal-to-noise ratios.

The resulting estimates control attenuation across frequency channels. The authors evaluate the method through speaker-independent digit recognition and compare it with Spectral Subtraction. This tests the proposed suppression procedure in a recognition setting, where the processed speech serves a downstream task. The abstract identifies the evaluation and comparison but does not state which method performed better.
neurips-2000-noise-suppression-based-on-.tldr: A neural network estimates local speech signal-to-noise ratios from auditory-inspired spectrograms to control frequency-specific noise suppression.

paragraphs: The paper describes three-dimensional integrated-circuit technology for neuromorphic circuits and the design of smart vision chips. Its engineering motivation is compact construction of chips that include a photodetector, with high-speed, general-purpose image processing as a potential application. Bringing light detection into the chip design makes physical integration part of the vision-system problem.

The authors propose three-dimensional large-scale integration as the fabrication approach. Their emphasis is on using the spatial organization of hardware as a resource when building neuromorphic systems. The biological inspiration therefore extends to structure as well as function: how a system is physically arranged matters alongside the operations it performs.

The contribution described in the abstract centers on the integration technology and chip designs. Their significance is the proposed connection between compact sensing hardware and structurally inspired neuromorphic circuits. High-speed image processing and new neuromorphic systems are presented as opportunities offered by the technology, rather than as quantified performance outcomes in the supplied account.
neurips-2000-smart-vision-chip-fabricate.tldr: The paper presents three-dimensional integration technology and smart vision chip designs aimed at compact, biologically inspired sensing hardware.

paragraphs: The paper proposes a cortical model for detecting motion in depth from binocular information. Its target is the selectivity of complex cells in visual cortex: how a modeled cell can respond strongly to particular motion toward or away from the observer, using information supplied by the two eyes.

The approach extends phase-based disparity estimation into time. Disparity describes a difference between the two eyes' views, and the model combines responses from disparity energy units to compute the total temporal derivative of changing disparity. This connects a representation of binocular differences to a representation of how those differences evolve.

To address physiological plausibility, the model combines binocular cells with different ocular dominance indices, meaning different relative contributions from the eyes. The resulting cortical units exhibit sharp selectivity for motion in depth, which the authors compare with published observations of real cortical cells. The stated result supports this hierarchy as a candidate computational account of motion-in-depth selectivity.
neurips-2001-a-hierarchical-model-of-com.tldr: A hierarchical binocular model combines disparity responses over time to produce sharply motion-in-depth-selective cortical units.

paragraphs: The information bottleneck method organizes data by grouping values of one variable while retaining information about another. Given a joint distribution over A and B, it constructs a variable T representing clusters of A that remain informative about B. This makes relevance to another variable part of the clustering problem.

The paper builds on a multivariate framework that allows several systems of partitions to be related to one another. Such a formulation concerns more than a single grouping considered in isolation: the relationships among multiple cluster systems become part of what the method must construct.

The authors introduce a family of simple agglomerative algorithms for this task. Agglomerative construction forms groups through merging, providing an algorithmic route to the interrelated partitions described by the framework. They analyze the algorithms' behavior and apply them to several real datasets. The contribution is a practical family of procedures for multivariate information-bottleneck organization, with analysis and applications rather than a stated universal performance advantage.
neurips-2001-agglomerative-multivariate-.tldr: The paper develops agglomerative algorithms that construct interrelated cluster systems within the multivariate information bottleneck framework.

paragraphs: The paper analyzes why sparse models can emerge from the Bayesian learning approach used by the relevance vector machine. In this framework, generalized linear model parameters have a particular Gaussian prior, and learning adjusts hyperparameters to maximize the marginal likelihood of the observed data.

The authors study the structure of that optimization objective. When considering an individual hyperparameter with the others fixed, they show that the marginal likelihood has a unique maximum that can be calculated in closed form. This gives a precise characterization of an individual adjustment within the larger learning problem; it does not establish a unique joint optimum for all hyperparameters.

They also derive a sparsity criterion. When that condition holds, the corresponding maximum is exactly equivalent to removing the associated model parameter. This explains pruning as a consequence of the marginal-likelihood objective under a stated condition. The analysis therefore links sparse solutions to the mathematical behavior of the learning criterion, making the removal of a parameter an explicit optimization result.
neurips-2001-analysis-of-sparse-bayesian.tldr: The paper characterizes individual hyperparameter optima in sparse Bayesian learning and derives a condition under which an optimum removes a model parameter.

paragraphs: The paper presents an algorithm that learns object components useful for classification. It uses support vector machines to judge image parts and grows those parts by minimizing theoretical bounds on classification error probability. The choice of components is therefore guided by their discriminative value within the learning procedure.

For face classification, the learned component classifiers feed into a second stage that combines them into a hierarchical SVM. The approach also uses three-dimensional morphable models for training and applies a maximum operation to each component classifier's output. The authors identify that operation as potentially relevant to biological accounts of visual recognition.

Experiments show considerable robustness when faces rotate in depth, changing the appearance of their parts. The results also suggest performance substantially better than other face detection systems. The stated evidence supports learning and combining component experts as a promising recognition strategy, while the comparison is presented as a suggestion from the experiments and the biological connection remains a possibility.
neurips-2001-categorization-by-learning-.tldr: A hierarchical SVM learns useful face parts and combines their predictions, showing robustness to depth rotations in experiments.

paragraphs: The paper investigates how eye movements might help refine the orientation preferences of cortical simple cells. These cells develop adjacent regions receiving different ON- and OFF-center inputs. Because visual experience depends on both the scene and how the eyes scan it, the authors examine movement as part of the developmental input.

Their computational model uses Hebbian synaptic plasticity and measures correlations among simulated cells while natural scenes are scanned. The scanning conditions represent saccades and the smaller movements that occur during fixation, including microsaccades, tremor, and drift. Static presentation of natural input provides another condition.

The activity patterns needed for quantitatively accurate development of separated ON and OFF subregions appeared during fixational movements. They did not appear under the modeled saccadic or static conditions. This result suggests that the small movements occurring during fixation may contribute to refinement of orientation selectivity. Its force comes from the comparison within the modeling framework, rather than a direct demonstration of developmental causation in animals.
neurips-2001-eye-movements-and-the-matur.tldr: Simulations suggest that fixational eye movements supply activity correlations that can support refinement of cortical orientation selectivity.

paragraphs: The paper addresses detection problems with a highly uneven balance of positive and negative examples, such as face detection. In this setting, the training goal includes retaining an extremely high proportion of positives. Minimizing overall classification error alone does not directly capture that priority.

The proposed detector arranges simple classifiers in a cascade. Each stage aims for a high detection rate while accepting a modest false positive rate. Together, the stages can produce a detector that is fast and has very few false positives. A new asymmetric variant of AdaBoost trains the stage classifiers to reflect the importance of high detection.

Face detection experiments show significant performance improvements from this training method over conventional AdaBoost. The completed system processes 15 frames per second, detects more than 90% of positives, and has a false positive rate of one in a million. These reported results demonstrate the combined approach in the tested domain, connecting asymmetric training goals with the behavior of the full cascade.
neurips-2001-fast-and-robust-classificat.tldr: Asymmetric AdaBoost trains a classifier cascade that achieves fast face detection with high detection and very low false positive rates.

paragraphs: The paper studies why partial cues sometimes retrieve a complete memory and sometimes fail, even when they contain enough information to identify it. In word-fragment experiments, the authors find that people complete short and long cues more accurately than medium-length cues. They also examine factors contributing to that pattern.

To model these behaviors, they develop a system that alternates between bottom-up and top-down computations. A Markov model of words connects the two directions of processing. It allows access to memory through a simple feature set and lets the bottom-up process calculate a probability distribution over possible word completions.

The computational model reproduces some of the flexibility and error patterns seen in human memory. Its significance is that a cue's identifying information and its ability to trigger retrieval are treated as different issues. The approach also connects word-fragment completion with models of visual perceptual completion through its probabilistic handling of partial evidence and interaction between processing directions.
neurips-2001-fragment-completion-in-huma.tldr: Word-fragment experiments and a probabilistic model explore why medium-length cues can produce more retrieval errors than shorter or longer cues.

paragraphs: The paper asks how groups of auditory neurons share information about sounds. The authors develop information-theoretic measures of group redundancy and apply them to two processing stations: the inferior colliculus and primary auditory cortex. Redundancy concerns how much information carried by neurons overlaps within a group.

They examine coding of acoustic segments and stimulus identity, finding differences between the two stations in both information content and group redundancy. The results provide direct evidence for reduced redundancy along the ascending auditory pathway. Under the single-spike coding scheme, significant redundancy effects occur only in groups containing more than ten cells, so measures restricted to pairs cannot reveal them.

This group-size result matters for how population coding is assessed: interactions visible across larger collections may escape pairwise analysis. The authors interpret the broader findings as suggesting a transformation from redundant lower-level representations toward cortical representations of rare, independent acoustic components. They propose that these components are useful for auditory scene analysis.
neurips-2001-group-redundancy-measures-r.tldr: Group-level information measures reveal auditory redundancy reduction and effects that pairwise neuron comparisons cannot detect.

paragraphs: The paper introduces a self-organizing map for navigating the semantic space of large text collections. Its central design choice is to organize the map on a hyperbolic plane, giving the spatial representation a geometry different from an ordinary flat map. The aim is to express complex relationships in language through spatial relationships.

The proposed hyperbolic SOM uses a regular tessellation of a space with constant negative curvature. A neighborhood around a point grows exponentially as it extends outward. The authors argue that this growth provides more freedom for mapping the information structure of text, making the geometry an active part of the representation.

Experiments show that the method can be applied successfully to text categorization and gives results comparable to other leading methods. These findings support hyperbolic organization as a workable approach to representing text collections. The reported comparison establishes competitive categorization performance, while the broader motivation is navigation through a spatial arrangement of semantic information.
neurips-2001-hyperbolic-self-organizing-.tldr: A self-organizing map on a hyperbolic plane organizes text semantics and achieves competitive text categorization results.

paragraphs: The paper examines how a support vector machine can use prior knowledge about transformations that should preserve a classification. Such knowledge is called invariance: an input may change in a known way while retaining the identity relevant to the task. Incorporating that knowledge can inform the representation used for learning.

An SVM's kernel determines how data are represented in a feature space. The authors therefore focus on putting invariance information into nonlinear kernels. Their technique extends earlier work and aims to make the chosen representation reflect known transformation relationships, connecting task knowledge directly to the kernel design.

The method is evaluated on digit recognition and outperforms the Virtual Support Vector method in that task. The comparison supports the proposed treatment of invariance in the reported setting. The contribution is both a technique for nonlinear kernels and evidence that this use of prior knowledge can improve recognition relative to the comparison method, without establishing superiority for every task or transformation.
neurips-2001-incorporating-invariances-i.tldr: A technique for incorporating transformation invariances into nonlinear SVM kernels outperforms Virtual Support Vectors on a digit recognition task.

paragraphs: The paper studies how to constrain the possible values of means and correlations in a Boltzmann machine. These statistics describe average unit behavior and relationships between units. The approach begins with upper and lower bounds on the partition function, the quantity used to normalize the model's probabilities.

The authors use those partition-function bounds to derive bounds on the statistics themselves. For networks with small weights, the resulting intervals are nontrivial: they cover only part of the full range from minus one to one. This gives information about where the true values can lie, even without specifying them exactly.

Experiments show reasonable bounding for weight magnitudes where mean-field expansions generally perform well. This places the practical finding in a qualified regime, rather than asserting equally informative bounds at all interaction strengths. The contribution is a connection between bounds on a global model quantity and restrictions on individual statistics, with empirical evidence that the restrictions can be useful for sufficiently small weights.
neurips-2001-means-correlations-and-boun.tldr: Partition-function bounds yield informative bounds on Boltzmann-machine means and correlations in a small-weight regime.

paragraphs: The paper examines a distinction within motivation: selecting among possible actions and deciding whether a particular response is worth making at all. A standard reinforcement-learning account frames motivation through predicted cumulative future reward, with actions competing according to the value of the states they lead to.

The authors argue that this account is incomplete in light of experimental work on the psychology and neurobiology of motivation. Animals often face a question about whether to execute one available response. The reviewed evidence suggests that this decision involves motivational processes with psychological and neural properties different from those involved in choosing among actions.

The paper describes and models these motivational systems and considers their interaction. Its contribution is to make the distinction part of a computational account, broadening what motivation must explain in instrumental conditioning. The evidence supports treating response execution and action choice as distinguishable processes, while the modeling addresses how those processes can interact within an account of motivated behavior.
neurips-2001-motivated-reinforcement-lea.tldr: The paper models the interaction between motivation to execute a response and motivation governing choice among actions.

paragraphs: The paper connects online learning with guarantees about predictive risk. Online algorithms update as examples arrive, while a generalization guarantee concerns how well a resulting predictor performs beyond the observations used in learning. The authors show how online classification and regression algorithms can yield hypotheses with data-dependent tail bounds on that risk.

A tail bound controls the probability of an unfavorable risk outcome, and a data-dependent bound incorporates information from the observed learning data. The framework applies to arbitrary online learning algorithms. The authors also establish the results without requiring complicated concentration-of-measure arguments, providing a comparatively direct route to the guarantees.

When specialized to concrete online algorithms, the framework gives bounds that are comparable to or better than the best known bounds in many cases. This is a qualified comparison, rather than an improvement claimed for every algorithm. The result matters because it supplies a general bridge from sequential learning procedures to probabilistic statements about their resulting predictors' performance.
neurips-2001-on-the-generalization-abili.tldr: A general framework turns online learning algorithms into predictors with data-dependent risk bounds that are competitive in many cases.

paragraphs: The paper presents a programmable hardware system for studying computation with spikes. It combines a silicon retina, a PIC microcontroller, and a transceiver chip containing integrate-and-fire neurons in a soft winner-take-all arrangement. The neuron circuit approximates a cortical microcircuit, while the retina supplies visual input.

The system changes neuronal computational properties through virtual connections to selected retinal pixels. Communication between chips uses asynchronous digital pulses in an event-driven protocol, resembling spike communication. This programmable wiring lets the authors implement both feedforward and feedback models of neurons tuned to visual orientation.

The analog spiking hardware matches experimental observations and digital simulations of continuous-valued neurons in the reported comparison. The authors also report real-time operation and computational time that does not grow with neuronal network size. These properties make the system a platform for exploring spike-based models through physical circuits, with orientation tuning serving as the demonstrated computation and virtual wiring supporting different configurations.
neurips-2001-orientation-selective-avlsi.tldr: Programmable spiking chips implement orientation-tuned neurons whose behavior matches experimental observations and continuous-valued simulations.

paragraphs: The paper develops a probabilistic approach to clustering data into a taxonomy. Each class has a probabilistic model describing how its data are generated, and nearby classes in the hierarchy are intended to reflect similarity. The task therefore includes learning both groups and the relationships organizing those groups.

The algorithm optimizes three connected elements: which cluster each instance belongs to, the probabilistic models attached to clusters, and the hierarchy's structure. It uses global optimization algorithms for the model and structure steps. The authors state that these choices reduce sensitivity to noise and the tendency to become trapped through exclusively local decisions, as in hierarchical agglomerative clustering.

The theoretical analysis establishes convergence to a local maximum of the joint likelihood of model and data. Global optimization within particular steps therefore does not imply a globally optimal final solution. Experiments use synthetic data as well as gene-expression and text data, demonstrating the framework's application across different kinds of hierarchical clustering problems.
neurips-2001-probabilistic-abstraction-h.tldr: A probabilistic clustering framework jointly learns assignments, class models, and taxonomy structure, with convergence to a local likelihood maximum.

paragraphs: The paper infers a subject's hand motion from recordings of multiple motor-cortex neurons. Training data pair neural firing with hand kinematics. A Bayesian model learns a nonparametric representation of the firing activity, and cross-validation is used to compare this representation with previous models.

During inference, the learned models for multiple cells define a non-Gaussian likelihood describing the neural evidence. This is combined with a prior over hand kinematics to obtain a posterior distribution over motion. A particle filter represents that distribution and updates and propagates it as successive neural observations arrive.

This approach maintains a probability distribution over possible movement instead of reducing the inference problem immediately to one trajectory. The authors compare it with traditional linear filtering methods, and the results suggest possible suitability for neural prosthetic applications. The stated application conclusion remains tentative: the contribution is a learned probabilistic decoding method and its evaluation, with prosthetic use identified as a promising direction.
neurips-2001-probabilistic-inference-of-.tldr: Bayesian firing models and particle filtering infer a distribution over hand motion from motor-cortex recordings.

paragraphs: The paper models a regularity in animal timing during delayed-reward conditioning. Responses measured for different time intervals align on a common curve after scaling by the relevant interval. This scalar property means that the timing pattern changes with the duration in a consistent, proportional way.

The proposed neural clock is an accumulator made of noisy, linear spiking neurons. Despite its simplicity, it produces the scalar property. The model has only three parameters and can be analyzed mathematically, allowing the authors to connect the clock's formulation with the timing behavior it generates.

When coupled with reinforcement learning, the clock simulates peak-procedure experiments. It reproduces both scalar timing and the observed pattern of covariances within individual trials. Matching these two kinds of structure matters because the model addresses relationships in single-trial behavior as well as the rescaled overall pattern. The result presents a compact computational account linking a noisy neural timing mechanism with learned responses to delayed reward.
neurips-2001-reinforcement-learning-and-.tldr: A three-parameter noisy neural clock coupled with reinforcement learning reproduces scalar timing and single-trial covariance patterns.

paragraphs: The paper proposes randomized approximations to speed up kernel principal component analysis. It addresses three distinct computational levels, covering the matrix used during training, the evaluation of kernel expansions, and the evaluation of the kernel function itself. This separates several places where kernel computation can be simplified.

For training, the methods use sampling and quantization of the Gram matrix, which contains kernel values between data points. For kernel expansions, they use randomized rounding. For individual kernel evaluations, they use random projections. Each technique targets a different operation within the broader method rather than requiring the same approximation at every level.

The authors provide sharp accuracy bounds for all three kinds of approximation. These bounds are central to the proposal because they characterize approximation quality alongside the intended computational savings. The abstract also presents the techniques under a common idea of replacing the kernel with a randomized kernel, although its final description of that unifying relationship is incomplete.
neurips-2001-sampling-techniques-for-ker.tldr: Three randomized approximation techniques target different costs in kernel PCA, each accompanied by accuracy bounds.

paragraphs: The paper studies noisy traveling-salesman problems in the plane whose random instances share an underlying structure. Its learning objective is to capture that common structure and use it when constructing solutions for new instances drawn from the same source. This makes a collection of related routing problems the basis for learning.

The authors use Gibbs sampling to compute average trajectories that estimate the shared structure. Doing this requires identifying the exact relationship between permutations and tours, so the representation of a route is part of the method. The resulting average trajectory serves as the model used on subsequent instances.

Experiments show that an average trajectory can estimate the underlying structure. They also reveal overfitting when the trajectory adapts too closely to one particular instance. The finding highlights the distinction between representing what related problems have in common and matching the noise in an individual problem. Generalization here is explicitly tied to new instances sampled from the same source.
neurips-2001-the-noisy-euclidean-traveli.tldr: Gibbs-sampled average tours can learn shared structure across noisy routing problems, but fitting one instance too closely causes overfitting.
